cover letter
At least 5 years of professional experience (2 years with Masters or Advanced degree).
Bachelor's degree and/or equivalent experience/training.

Demonstrated experience developing or carrying out projects addressing ethical, societal, or governance questions related to science, technology, or health. Relevant experience may include public or community engagement, participatory research, ethical or philosophical analysis, policy or governance research, qualitative or mixed-methods research, or related approaches.
Experience designing or facilitating public, community, or stakeholder engagement related to science, technology, health, or public policy.
Demonstrated judgment, discretion, and cultural awareness when working on ethically sensitive or contested issues and with people whose experiences or perspectives may differ from one’s own.
Experience with philosophical or normative ethical analysis, policy analysis, governance research, or other analytical approaches to questions at the intersection of science and society.
Experience with participatory research, community co-design, deliberative engagement, dialogue, interviews, focus groups, surveys, or other qualitative or mixed-methods approaches.
Experience working with scientists or research institutions to integrate ethical reflection, community knowledge, public perspectives, or governance considerations into research and decision-making.

Experience producing reports, articles, ethical frameworks, policy resources, toolkits, workshops, convenings, public scholarship, or other outputs intended for use beyond a single academic discipline.

With support from the John Templeton Foundation, the Kavli Center is hosting an 18-month Civic Science Fellowship focused on emerging frontiers in neuroscience. This is a full-time, limited staff position for a researcher or practitioner who can lead a research and engagement project from initial design through delivery and evaluation. The Civic Science Fellow in Neuroscience, Kavli Center for Ethics, Science, and the Public connects scientific research with analysis of ethical questions and meaningful engagement with publics and communities, helping scientists and other participants consider not only what is becoming technically possible, but what is morally permissible and societally desirable, while research directions and norms are still taking shape.
Project Planning and Execution - 40%

This position is part of the national Civic Science Fellows program, a network of fellows, host organizations, funders, and other partners working across sectors to strengthen connections between science, communities, and civic life. Fellows are embedded in host organizations to develop and pilot civic science projects while participating in a national cohort that provides shared learning, professional development, and opportunities to build relationships across the field.

Collaboratively plan, co-design, manage, and execute one primary civic science project aligned with the Kavli Center’s mission and the fellowship’s neuroscience focus. Develop and maintain an 18-month work plan, timeline, and milestones; conduct and synthesize the research and analysis needed to advance the project; coordinate Center colleagues and external collaborators; and build relationships with relevant experts, communities, and other stakeholders. Design and implement the project’s reciprocal engagement component, either directly or by identifying and working with collaborators who bring relevant expertise.

This fellowship builds on the success of our previous Civic Science Fellow and the resulting Wired Minds project (kavlicenter.berkeley.edu/wired-minds). Through Wired Minds, we sought to understand the macroethical practices and beliefs of U.S. neuroscientists and created spaces where Bay Area neuroscientists and members of the public could explore together the ethical and societal implications of brain-computer interfaces. The incoming Civic Science Fellow will have the opportunity to expand upon this work or to develop a complementary line of work related to areas such as neurotechnology and mental privacy; technologies that write to or intervene in the brain; or emerging questions about mind and moral status raised by brain organoids, animal communication, or other areas of research.
Project Outputs and Dissemination - 25%

While the specific project and work products will be co-designed with the selected Fellow, potential research questions include how new abilities to read from or intervene in neural systems reshape concepts such as agency, dignity, and responsibility; how scientists should navigate moral uncertainty when research challenges established ideas about mind or moral status; and how interdisciplinary and public engagement can inform scientific decision-making before technologies are fully entrenched.

Develop and disseminate useful outputs from the project. Translate research and engagement findings into accessible and useful forms for relevant audiences, which may include reports or articles, ethical frameworks or guiding questions, workshops or convenings, public-facing resources, and practical tools. Document and evaluate the project’s methods, outcomes, and lessons and prepare materials that will allow effective approaches to be adapted or sustained in future work.

Methods may draw on literature and landscape research; interviews or other qualitative inquiry; philosophical, humanistic, or social scientific approaches to examining ethical and societal questions; public or stakeholder deliberation; engagement with communities; and collaboration with scientists and trainees. Whatever its specific focus, the project will include a substantive, reciprocal engagement component involving relevant publics, communities, or other stakeholders. The Fellow may design and facilitate this work directly or bring in collaborators to contribute relevant expertise. Potential outputs include research findings, ethical frameworks or guiding questions, convenings, public-facing resources, and practical tools for researchers or institutions. The Fellow will document and evaluate the work so that useful methods and lessons can inform future projects at the Kavli Center and across the civic science field.
Cohort and Community Participation - 20%

In addition to leading the fellowship project, the Fellow will contribute to the Kavli Center’s development as a place where civic science approaches are developed, tested, and integrated into broader work at the intersection of science and society. Drawing on lessons from their project and the national Civic Science Fellows network, the Fellow will help strengthen the Center’s capacity for civic science through selected programs, convenings, partnerships, and other interdisciplinary initiatives. The fellowship project will remain the Fellow’s primary responsibility.

Participate actively in the national Civic Science Fellows cohort and the Kavli Center fellowship community, including learning activities, training, peer exchange, works-in-progress sessions, and professional development. Bring relevant learning from these experiences back to the Kavli Center and incorporate it into the Fellow’s project and broader contributions.

The Fellow will report to and work closely with the Kavli Center’s Executive Director, who will provide ongoing guidance and thought partnership. The Fellow will also have opportunities to engage and collaborate with faculty and other experts in neuroscience, ethics, social science, and public engagement through the Kavli Center and will participate in the Center’s interdisciplinary community of graduate and postdoctoral fellows.
Center Capacity Building - 15%

Help strengthen the Kavli Center’s capacity as a home for civic science by applying relevant approaches and lessons from the fellowship project to selected Center programs and initiatives. This may include helping to adapt engagement methods and tools for other projects, contributing to convenings or fellowship programming, developing relationships with potential partners, and sharing civic science practices with Center colleagues.

We welcome candidates whose experience lies in public or community engagement, ethics or philosophy, social science, science and technology studies, public policy or governance, or related fields. Candidates are not expected to bring expertise in all of these areas.
Proficiency with common office and online collaboration tools used for project coordination, research, and multi-stakeholder engagement.
Ability to review and synthesize complex scientific information and ethical, societal, or policy perspectives, and to identify important questions, tensions, and implications.
Knowledge of, or demonstrated ability to learn about, contemporary neuroscience and its ethical and societal dimensions, with a particular focus on fundamental or discovery neuroscience.

Strong project management skills, including the ability to turn an open-ended question into a focused work plan, coordinate collaborators and activities, adapt as the work develops, and deliver results within a fixed timeframe.
Ability to work productively across disciplines and forms of expertise, build relationships with academic and non-academic partners, and seek and incorporate feedback.
Excellent written and oral communication skills, including the ability to communicate complex ideas accurately and accessibly to different audiences.
Ability to work both independently and collaboratively in an interdisciplinary environment.
